clue.text: Source material for Adam's novel

parts.note: reads as the research behind some author's book, but means the stuff God shaped the first man from in Genesis, which is also the title of an Evelyn Waugh novel

explanation.surface: A literary critic asks what inspired a writer called Adam to produce his novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis has Adam formed from the dust of the ground; Waugh's 1934 novel takes its title from a line of Eliot's The Waste Land.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both the title of Evelyn Waugh's novel and a small heap of the earth from which Adam was made.

clue.text: War artist's genre?

parts.note: a war artist would depict fighting, and fighting is another word for battle scenes; the question mark flags the style of Jackson Pollock, whose drip technique has this name

explanation.surface: Someone asks what kind of pictures an official war artist produces.
explanation.walkthrough: Pollock's style of flinging and dripping paint is named for physical movement, but read literally it suggests pictures of combat.
explanation.definitionFit: Battle is military combat, so pictures of it fit a war artist, while the name also labels the abstract expressionist drip style.

clue.text: Bitter psyche in a supremo

indicators.note: in says the word for psyche is placed inside the abbreviation for the supremo

parts.note: CIC is short for commander-in-chief, the supreme commander
the id is the instinctive part of the psyche in Freudian theory

explanation.surface: A sour mood is found in the mind of an overbearing boss.
explanation.walkthrough: CIC (commander-in-chief) is a common crossword stand-in for a supreme leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Acidic tastes are sharp and sour, and a bitter remark can likewise be called acidic or caustic.

clue.text: Ruminant raising two offspring

indicators.note: two asks for the reversed word to appear twice in a row
in a down clue, raising means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a kid is a child, one's offspring

explanation.surface: A grazing animal is bringing up a couple of young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' turns KID upwards into DIK, and 'two' doubles it. 'Raising two offspring' looks like a picture of parenthood.
explanation.definitionFit: The dik-dik is a tiny African antelope, and like all antelopes it chews the cud as a ruminant.

clue.text: Broke a Latin rule, no two ways about it!

indicators.note: something broken has its pieces scattered, so the letters of the following words are reassembled in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A schoolboy breaks a rule of Latin grammar, and that's that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broke' rearranges A LATIN RULE. The definition is playful: one-sided means there is only one way, so 'no two ways about it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Unilateral describes action taken by one side only, which jokingly allows no second way about it.

clue.text: See 1
Countenance discomfort with fright

parts.note: a countenance is a face
an ache is a dull discomfort or pain

explanation.surface: A painful expression shown by someone who has had a scare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fright' looks like the cause of the pained face, but it is the definition: in British slang a fright or a face-ache is a person with an ugly or miserable face.
explanation.definitionFit: In British informal use both words describe someone who looks unattractive or perpetually glum.

clue.text: Too fond of the squaw in our Sioux regiment

indicators.note: to regiment is to drill and reorganise, so the letters of the preceding words are marshalled into a new order

explanation.surface: A Native American warrior band is accused of being too devoted to women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regiment' rearranges OUR SIOUX; it looks like a noun for a body of soldiers but works as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Uxorious describes a husband excessively devoted to his wife; squaw is the dated, now offensive word for a Native American wife.

clue.text: Classic results from aquatic parturition?

parts.note: a water birth would produce infants delivered in a pool, and the Victorian children's classic by Charles Kingsley bears that name

explanation.surface: A question about what a birthing pool produces, dressed up as a literary query.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley's 1863 fantasy is about a chimney sweep turned into a tiny river creature; the question mark warns that the birth is a literal reading of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley's novel is a recognised classic, and newborns delivered in a birthing pool could be described by its title.

clue.text: Will oneself to exercise?

parts.note: reads as forcing yourself into a workout, but the phrase also means to decide or deem appropriate, here punned as imagining yourself in good shape

explanation.surface: Someone tries to summon the willpower to go to the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means to choose or see fit; read literally it suggests getting in shape by thought alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to decide or deem proper, which is close to willing, and literally suggests believing yourself healthy.

clue.text: How bugs emerge new from hedge

indicators.note: from here means taken away from, so the abbreviation for new is removed from the word for hedge

parts.note: to hedge a field is to enclose it

explanation.surface: Insects are crawling out of a recently planted hedgerow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new from hedge' looks like a description of where bugs come out; it means N removed from ENCLOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To eclose is the entomologists' verb for an insect breaking out of its pupal case or egg.

clue.text: Old dress length holding in a model

indicators.note: holding means the first group of letters wraps around the words in a

parts.note: rig is clothing, a dress or outfit

explanation.surface: An old dress of a certain length is worn by a fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: IN A, as written, goes inside ORIGL, just before the final L.
explanation.definitionFit: An original is the first version from which copies are made, so it serves as a model or pattern.

clue.text: Whitbread Prize winner

parts.note: suggests an author who won the Whitbread book award, but means the British javelin thrower surnamed Whitbread, who won medals and prizes

explanation.surface: A literary award announcement names this year's winner.
explanation.walkthrough: Fatima Whitbread was a British javelin world champion in 1987; the Whitbread Prize was a major British book award, which sends the solver looking for a novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: The athlete with that surname won world and Olympic medals, so she is literally a Whitbread who won prizes.

clue.text: Desirée thus bedded by tennis ace Murphy

parts.note: a seed is a top-ranked tennis player placed in the draw
murphy is slang for a potato, from the Irish surname

explanation.surface: A woman called Desirée is seduced by a star tennis player named Murphy.
explanation.walkthrough: Desirée is a red-skinned potato variety, and tubers planted in a bed to grow new plants are seed potatoes; the surface reads as a bedroom scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Desirée is a variety of potato, and one planted in a bed to raise a crop is a tuber kept for sowing.

clue.text: Safe harbour for a Cambridge eight

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
to harbour someone is to house or shelter them

explanation.surface: A rowing crew from Cambridge finds a secure place to moor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe harbour' looks like one phrase for a port; it splits into two pieces. Peterhouse is the oldest Cambridge college, and its rowing crew is an eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Peterhouse is a Cambridge college that puts a rowing eight on the river, so its name stands for that crew.

clue.text: See 1
Anthropophagite swapping head for heart of the Elephant Man

indicators.note: the leading letter of the word for a man-eater is exchanged for another letter

parts.note: an anthropophagite is a man-eater

indicators.note: heart of picks the central letter of the word the

explanation.surface: A man-eater trades places with the core of the famous disfigured Victorian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swapping head for' replaces the first letter C of CANNIBAL with H, the middle of 'the'. Hannibal led elephants over the Alps, and Hannibal Lecter is a fictional cannibal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Carthaginian general famously crossed the Alps with war elephants, so he is the elephant man of history.

clue.text: Creature with knobbly knees and wobbly bot

indicators.note: knobbly suggests something lumpy and misshapen, so these letters are jumbled
wobbly suggests unsteadiness, a second signal that the letters are rearranged together

explanation.surface: An animal with bony knees and a shaky backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The two signals 'knobbly' and 'wobbly' together jumble KNEES and BOT as one pool; the steenbok is a small African antelope.
explanation.definitionFit: The steenbok is a small antelope of southern and eastern Africa, so it is an example of a creature.

clue.text: Trailblazers take advantage roughly

indicators.note: roughly suggests imprecise handling, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: R stands for recipe, Latin for take, as written on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Pioneers seize an opportunity without much finesse.
explanation.walkthrough: R, for 'take' (Latin recipe), joins ADVANTAGE and 'roughly' shuffles the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: The avant-garde are the innovators at the forefront of art or ideas, those who blaze new trails.

clue.text: Such law written in stone

parts.note: the law given to Moses was inscribed on stone tablets, and a picture made of small stones set in cement shares the same adjective

explanation.surface: A statement about a rule so fixed it might as well be carved in rock.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ten Commandments were written on stone tablets given to Moses; the same word names art made from stone tesserae.
explanation.definitionFit: The law of Moses carries this adjective, and the same word names pictures assembled from small pieces of stone.

clue.text: He abdicated a long way from old England etc

parts.note: far means at a great distance
England with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland makes up the UK

explanation.surface: An exiled monarch left power a long way from his former English home.
explanation.walkthrough: King Farouk of Egypt abdicated in 1952 after a military coup.
explanation.definitionFit: Farouk, the last effective king of Egypt, gave up his throne in 1952, so he is a man who abdicated.

clue.text: See 8
Non-starters, when the ayes have it unanimously

definitions.meaning: flat refusals, things that will never happen

definitions.text: when the ayes have it unanimously
definitions.meaning: in a parliamentary vote, if everyone says aye there are no votes against

explanation.surface: A commentator dismisses certain proposals in a vote where everyone agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: In Parliament the votes are 'ayes' and 'noes'; a unanimous aye vote leaves no noes at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphatic refusals are things that will never go ahead, and a unanimous yes vote literally has zero votes against.

clue.text: "Oh no!", she's announced, "Arkwright's lad rammed a port"

indicators.note: rammed means pressed up hard against, so the letter a is pushed right up beside the son's name

parts.note: the cry Oh no sounds like Ono, so she is Yoko Ono
Noah was the wright who built the Ark, and Ham was one of his sons

explanation.surface: A woman cries out as a shopkeeper's boy crashes a vehicle into a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arkwright' suggests the shopkeeper of the British sitcom Open All Hours, but here it is Noah, wright (builder) of the Ark; his son is HAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Yokohama is a major Japanese seaport on Tokyo Bay, an example of a port.

clue.text: Swallow returning East, partly by the same fast route

annotationWithheld.why: Swallow returning East, partly by the same fast route (6): IMBIBE reversed is E + BIB + MI, and M1 for 'fast route' and E for 'East' fit, but no clue word gives BIB; 'partly by the same' seems to describe BIB reading the same both ways rather than supply it
annotationWithheld.clue: Swallow returning East, partly by the same fast route

clue.text: Film a car on Italian part of the course

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A director shoots a car scene on an Italian stretch of a racetrack.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaroni is a pasta, served as one course of an Italian meal.

clue.text: Oh, slick Kate! Ego shattered? Don't stay long on the shelf!

definitions.text: Don't stay long on the shelf!

indicators.note: shattered means broken into pieces, so the letters of the preceding words are reassembled

explanation.surface: A smooth woman named Kate is warned, after a blow to her pride, not to stay unmarried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shattered' rearranges OH SLICK KATE EGO. 'On the shelf' suggests a spinster, but here it is goods on a shop shelf.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods that sell very quickly are said to sell like freshly made griddle cakes, never lingering in stock.
